title: Lowering blood cholesterol to prevent heart disease. National Institutes of Health Consensus Development Conference Statement
authors: National Institutes of Health Consensus Development Conference
result: Conference of 10 to 12 December 1984. The panel stated that defining abnormal blood cholesterol by the 95th percentile of the population is unreasonable for the United States, that levels above 200 and 230 mg/dl are associated with increased risk of premature coronary heart disease, representing about 50% of US adults, and defined two treatable categories from Lipid Research Clinics percentiles: moderate risk (75th to 90th percentile) and high risk (90th percentile or above). Thresholds for treatment: age 20 to 29, above 200 mg/dl (moderate) and 220 mg/dl (high); 30 to 39, above 220 and 240 mg/dl; 40 and over, above 240 and 260 mg/dl. It recommended diet first (30% of energy from fat, saturated fat 10% or less, cholesterol 250 to 300 mg/day), drugs only after a careful trial of diet, and a goal of below 200 mg/dl (below 180 mg/dl under age 30) for the entire adult population. It stated that the clinical trials were too limited to settle effects on overall mortality, but that it was reasonable to presume a reduction; that each 1% reduction in blood cholesterol yields about a 2% reduction in coronary heart disease rates; and that the Lipid Research Clinics trial showed a 19% reduction in coronary heart disease with a 9% fall in cholesterol on cholestyramine.
